---

### Added

- **Invite a friend into a server you run, from the conversation.** Their
  profile in the friends list now offers every server you own, and one press
  sends them a way in — as a message in your conversation, with a Join button
  on it, rather than a ticket to copy out and paste somewhere. A gated server
  admits them at the same moment, which only its owner can do; an admin gets
  told so rather than sending an invitation that would not work.

- **A window per conversation, in the two-window shape.** Clicking somebody in
  the friends window used to replace the list with the conversation — in the
  one window you keep open beside your work to see who is around. It pops out
  instead: one window per person, raised again rather than duplicated if you
  ask twice, and the list stays a list.

- **Private channels, and removal that actually removes.** A server's write
  capability is shared by everyone in it and cannot be recalled, so removing
  somebody has only ever stopped them being *believed*: their entries are
  dropped by every reader, and they go on receiving everything written
  afterwards. That is a property of the substrate, not a bug — the way out is
  to stop writing anything they can read.

  A channel can now be created private. What is said in it is sealed under a
  key held by the people in the server, filed in the same document, one sealed
  copy per account. Removing somebody mints a new key for everyone else, so
  from that moment they sync the same entries and find bytes. What was said
  before stays readable to them: they already have it, and no rotation reaches
  into a copy somebody is holding.

  The sealing is X25519 over the same curve the accounts already live on —
  their public key as a Montgomery point, our secret as the scalar — with
  ChaCha20-Poly1305 over the result. Which means a channel key follows the
  *account*: it reaches every device you own, and a device joining your account
  gets the channels with it.

  Being admitted to a gated server hands over the keys in the same breath, so
  being let in means being able to read. A channel whose key you do not hold is
  listed with a mark saying so, rather than opening empty.

### Changed

- **Presence is said, not written.** A status used to be an entry in the
  server's document: stored for ever by every member, gossiped to all of them,
  and written into *every* server you are in, to describe something that
  expired minutes later. It now goes on a gossip topic beside each server —
  broadcast when you join, when it changes, when somebody new arrives, and
  every thirty seconds; believed for seventy-five, and then you are simply not
  there. Nothing is stored, and a device that vanishes stops being here
  without having to announce it.

  The claims are signed, because gossip is authenticated hop by hop and the
  peer that hands you a message is not the peer that wrote it. Each carries
  the certificate binding a device to its account and a signature over the
  server, the account, the status and the time — so a relaying peer cannot
  edit one in flight, and one heard on one server cannot be replayed on
  another.

- **Conversations sync while the person is there, not all day.** Every
  friendship held two documents open for the whole session — one written by
  each side — which is two subscriptions, two tasks and two swarms per friend
  whether or not either of you was around. A conversation can only travel
  while both people are online, so holding them open the rest of the time
  bought nothing. They start when your friend appears, stop when they go, and
  open on demand when you read or write. What was said is on your disk either
  way; this is about the swarm, not the history.

- **History goes back further than the last two hundred messages.** Opening a
  channel read the newest two hundred and stopped there: scrolling up reached
  the end of what had been loaded, not the end of what was said. It pages now,
  a hundred at a time, as you scroll — and holds your place while it does,
  which means measuring the list either side of the insertion rather than
  guessing at it.

  Paged by a cursor rather than an offset, because an offset moves: a message
  arriving while somebody reads shifts every page behind it by one, which is
  how a paged list quietly skips things.

- **Unfriending moved to where the name is.** The conversation header carried
  an *Unfriend* button beside a line saying whether they were online, which is
  the dot's job. Both are gone; right-clicking somebody in either friends list
  offers it, with a confirmation that says plainly what unfriending does and
  what it cannot undo.

- **Three things that grew all session now have a ceiling.** Nothing here
  changes what the app does; it changes what it holds onto while doing it.

  Avatars crossed the IPC as base64 and were kept as strings for the life of
  the session, one per person in every server — so a picture somebody uploaded
  at eight megabytes was eleven megabytes of held text, permanently. The cache
  is now bounded by its own size rather than by nothing, and drops the least
  recently drawn picture when it goes over; the bytes are in this machine's
  blob store, so what that costs is a local read.

  Message history was capped per channel and uncapped in channels, so every
  channel opened in a session kept a thousand messages for the rest of it.
  Twelve channels are held now, never the one on screen, and a channel dropped
  reloads from the document it was always read from.

  Cards of friends of friends were opened and synced at startup — up to two
  hundred documents, each a subscription and a task — to answer a question
  nobody had asked. They are opened when the discovery list is, and the cap is
  forty.

- **Presence goes where it can be seen.** Going idle wrote an entry into every
  server this account is in — each one a permanent record in a replicated
  document, gossiped to everybody in that server, to tell people who are not
  connected something they cannot see anyway. A member who is unreachable
  already reads as offline whatever their entry claims, so those writes were
  carrying nothing.

  A status now reaches the servers where somebody is actually connected, and a
  server nobody was in gets it the moment somebody arrives. Joining or leaving
  a voice channel still writes to that server whether or not anyone is
  listening: a room that goes on showing somebody who left is worse than a
  write nobody reads.

### Fixed

- **Every server keeps syncing, not just the last one you opened.** A server
  syncs through a gossip swarm of its members, and joining that swarm needs
  somewhere to start. iroh-docs remembers peers it has synced with and dials
  those, which is enough for a server used recently and not enough for one
  that has not been opened in a while — an empty or stale list means the
  swarm never forms, so that server quietly stops updating and your presence
  in it never arrives, while every other server looks fine.

  Each server now starts from the devices its own member entries name. Those
  are already on this disk, they cannot go stale the way a peer cache does,
  and ids are enough — discovery finds the addresses.

- **Leaving a server offers the way back in.** A friend's card lists the
  servers they publish and says whether you are in each one. That answer was
  read once, so after leaving one the row still said *Open* — which opened
  something this device no longer had, where nothing could be sent. The row
  now reads what the device actually holds, and leaving re-reads the lists it
  changes the meaning of.

- **A server whose members are all offline has a name again.** It came up as
  "Syncing…" and stayed there, because a server's name lives in the server's
  own document and a document is readable only while somebody who holds it is
  online — most visibly for a friend's server joined from their card. The name
  is now kept locally the moment anything can say it: on creating, on joining,
  from the card that published it, or from the device that handed it over in a
  pairing. It is refreshed whenever the document can be read, so a rename is
  not frozen at the day you joined, and "Syncing…" now means nothing has ever
  been able to tell us.
